blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights CHERIABI as an impressive effort to adapt a complete C/C++/assembly software stack (including FreeBSD, PostgreSQL, and hundreds of libraries) to use hardware-enforced capability-based pointers for memory protection. The key insight is whether strong pointer-based protection can be practical for large-scale C codebases with minimal changes and reasonable performance overhead. CHERIABI achieves this with a 6.8% slowdown, far better than tools like Address Sanitizer (50% overhead). The paper introduces the 'principle of intentional use' alongside least privilege, ensuring privileges are explicitly invoked. The implementation extends CHERI capabilities to userspace, system calls, and kernel interactions, eliminating legacy pointer vulnerabilities. Evaluation shows high compatibility (most programs require no changes) and strong memory-safety benefits, detecting nearly all injected safety violations while maintaining performance.
paper_title: CHERI ABI: Enforcing Valid Pointer Provenance and Minimizing Pointer Privilege in the POSIX C Run-Time Environment
paper_abstract: The CHERI architecture allows pointers to be implemented as capabilities (rather than integer virtual addresses) in a manner that is compatible with, and strengthens, the semantics of the C language. In addition to the spatial protections offered by conventional fat pointers, CHERI capabilities offer strong integrity, enforced provenance validity, and access monotonicity. When the process model, user-kernel interactions, dynamic linking, and memory management are all considered, we observe that simple derivation of architectural capabilities is insufficient to describe appropriate access to memory. We bridge this conceptual gap with a notional abstract capability that describes the accesses that should be allowed at a given point in execution, whether in the kernel or userspace. To investigate this notion at scale, we describe the first adaptation of a full C-language operating system (FreeBSD) with an enterprise database (PostgreSQL) for complete spatial and referential memory safety.
